extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and lawmakers interested in political philosophy, lawmaking, and religion policy
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance for legislators and analysts on crafting laws about religion, toleration, and the civic effects of laws; includes cautions about penal laws, religious change, and how laws shape national manners and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws shape moeurs and national character
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment: 'Comment les lois peuvent contribuer à former les moeurs, les manières et le caractère d'une nation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators must recognize that laws do not merely reflect customs but actively form manners, passions, and civic character. When drafting laws, consider their long-term effects on citizens' dispositions (independence, pride, politeness, industry, public spirit), political factioning, and social roles (e.g., status of clergy, role of soldiers). Examples in the text show predictable social outcomes (commerce, naval strength, politeness, literary tone) arising from particular legal regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft laws in accordance with national conditions (climate, situation, economy)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Je ne dis point que le climat n'ait produit, en grande partie, les lois... mais je dis que les moeurs et les manières de cette nation devraient avoir un grand rapport à ses lois.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawmakers should account for environmental, economic and social conditions when designing institutions and statutes; mismatches between law and national circumstances produce incoherent or unstable customs. The text argues for correspondence between laws and the nation's material and social realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require mutual toleration when multiple religions are permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Lorsque les lois d'un État ont cru devoir souffrir plusieurs religions, il faut qu'elles les obligent aussi à se tolérer entre elles.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil law that allows multiple religions should also impose obligations of mutual non-interference among religious groups. A citizen's compliance entails not only refraining from agitating the state but also not troubling other citizens. Rationale: repressed religions tend to become repressive once freed; legal mutual toleration reduces cycles of persecution and social conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: If state controls admission of new religions, prefer non-establishment when satisfied; tolerate if already established
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Quand on est maître de recevoir dans un État une nouvelle religion, ou de ne la pas recevoir, il ne faut pas l'y établir; quand elle y est établie, il faut la tolérer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the civil power has authority over admitting new creeds, the prudent policy (per the author) is to refuse establishment of a new religion if the state is content with the existing one; conversely, if a religion is already established, civil law must tolerate it. This is framed as a fundamental principle of political religion law in the text (Chap. X).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid penal laws concerning religion; prefer attraction not coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Il faut éviter les lois pénales en fait de religion... Règle générale: en fait de changement de religion, les invitations sont plus fortes que les peines.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penal statutes aimed at belief foster fear but are counterproductive: religious penalties interact with religious sanctions and can make souls 'atroces' or hardened. To encourage religious change or conformity, use inducements—improved fortunes, comforts, and other positive incentives—rather than punishments. Historical examples (e.g., persecutions in Japan) show persecutions provoke resistance; long, wearing penalties may be less inflammatory but still destructive in the long run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing the dominant religion risks political instability and revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Un prince qui entreprend dans son État de détruire ou de changer la religion dominante s'expose beaucoup... La révolution vient de ce qu'un État ne change pas de religion, de moeurs et de manières dans un instant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulers attempting to alter an established religion endanger the state's stability because religion is entangled with constitution, customs, and climate. Sudden legal imposition of a new religion undermines citizens' confidence in laws and government, produces bad citizens and bad faithful, and frequently provokes major unrest or revolution—especially in regimes where the change contradicts the population's settled moeurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persecution begets reciprocal persecution
rubrics_metrics.description: 'C'est un principe, que toute religion qui est réprimée devient elle-même réprimante.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and political principle: repressed religious groups, once able, are likely to persecute those who persecuted them. Therefore, laws that repress religious minorities produce future cycles of repression and retaliation; this should inform decisions about toleration and penal provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil laws should prevent religions from disturbing citizens, not merely the state
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Un citoyen ne satisfait point aux lois en se contentant de ne pas agiter le corps de l'État: il faut encore qu'il ne trouble pas quelque citoyen que ce soit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond maintaining public order, statutes concerning religion should explicitly prohibit acts by religious groups that harm other citizens. The duty of citizens under law includes respecting other individuals' peace and rights, not only refraining from sedition against the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: In free regimes, permit broad speech and private expression unless expressly forbidden
rubrics_metrics.description: '...un citoyen, dans cet État, dirait et écrirait tout ce que les lois ne lui ont pas défendu expressément de dire ou d'écrire.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing rules for free societies, the presumption is liberty of expression: individuals will say and write whatever the laws do not explicitly forbid. Lawmakers should therefore be deliberate about the scope of prohibitions and mindful of effects on public discourse, faction, and civic temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer reforms by persuasion and moral suasion over forced corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: (Implied across chapters: clergy seeking to persuade rather than coerce; reforms should be by attraction.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where institutional or religious abuses exist, the better course is persuasion and improving social conditions rather than coercive suppression. The clergy, lacking coercive power, should seek to instruct and persuade (producing 'de très bons ouvrages') rather than relying on force; similarly, civil reform should favor non-coercive measures to avoid creating perverse incentives and inhuman outcomes.
